name: Yusuf Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't sell anything and we're not tied to any company or party. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run a claims team at a big home and car insurer, eleven handlers on the third floor of our office near the train station. I'm in by eight, I check the overnight queue, and I hand out the tricky claims to the people who can handle them. Most of my day is approvals, a stand-up meeting at half nine, and listening to someone whose customer has shouted at them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. Bilal has been there fifteen years and still teaches me things, and I like being the one who sticks up for the team when head office sends down another target. What wears me out is the reporting. Every Friday I fill in the same weekly spreadsheet for my boss, and I'm still not sure anyone reads it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Amira, she's a nurse on a children's ward, and we rent a flat ten minutes from the office. We've saved about nine months of money, mostly because we're careful and neither of us likes owing anything. I'm not a gadget person. My phone is four years old and I've never once typed a question into one of those AI chat tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At work I'd say the claims job still needs a human who can read a customer and tell when a story doesn't add up. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about how the tech firms oversold it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays my job, and I'd be relieved. The insurer already bought a tool last year that sorts simple windscreen claims, and it hasn't taken a single seat on my team. If that's the ceiling, I can live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, managing the team and fighting for their pay rise in the spring review. I'd keep putting money aside every month, the same three hundred a month we always do. I probably wouldn't bother learning the new tools if they only shave off ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm being honest with you. It's the world I already know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the windscreen tool hasn't taken a seat. What does it actually do to your team's day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes the boring ones, the cracked windscreen with a photo and a receipt. My handlers moan that now every claim they touch is a hard one, so the day feels heavier, not lighter. Bilal (a senior claims handler) says it's like a shop that only lets you serve the angry customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still worries you, even with AI going nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me. Our rent went up eight percent this year, but we can carry that. The thing I'd watch is head office, because they cut a team in the north last year to save money, and that had nothing to do with AI.

say: I'd tell people a **claims handler** still needs to read a customer, and the hype missed that.
I'd share posts saying the **tech firms** oversold it, though I rarely post anything myself.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because my job stays mine and nothing on my team changes.
The **windscreen tool** shows the ceiling: it sorts easy claims but takes no seats.
do: Keep managing the eleven handlers and push for their **pay rise** at the spring review.
Keep saving the usual **three hundred a month** with my partner Amira.
feel: Mostly **calm**, and a little smug that the world stays the one I know.
S0.quote: Bilal (a senior claims handler) says it's like a shop that only lets you serve the angry customers.
fieldNote: He has a real **cushion** and a trusted role, so the plateau leaves him secure.
He noticed that automating **easy claims** makes his handlers' days harder, not lighter.
His worry here is **head office cuts**, not AI, and even that feels distant to him.

steps.text: Keep running the claims team and argue for the spring pay rise
Keep paying three hundred a month into the joint savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company owes the handlers a proper plan, not a memo. At work I'd ask in every meeting what happens to the people whose checks get moved to software. Online I'd probably back the union's line, because the union at our place is small but it's the only one asking the right questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd show. Checking claims is exactly what this card says goes first, and my whole team checks claims. If eleven handlers become five, they don't need me, they need someone who can run the software, and that someone isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly instead of just paying the fee and ignoring the emails. I'd sit down with Amira and agree that we stop putting money into anything risky and keep the cash. I suppose I'd have to go on the company course for the new claims system, even though I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting under me. I'm not panicking, because we've got the money, but I'd be lying awake running the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bilal, without a doubt. He's fifty-one, he knows more about claims than the whole system, and he's never written a report on a computer in his life. If they cut the team, my boss Carol will look at his age and his speed on screen, and that's the end of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate the course. What would make you go anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, really. If I'm the manager who won't touch the new system, I'm the first name on the list. I'd go, I'd sit at the back, and I'd learn just enough to keep my seat.

say: I'd say the company owes the handlers a **proper plan**, not a memo.
I'd back the **union's line** online, because it's the only group asking the right questions.
think: **Checking claims** is exactly what goes first, and my whole team checks claims.
If eleven handlers become five, they need a **software person**, not me.
do: Join the **union** properly and start reading the emails I used to ignore.
Move our savings out of anything risky and **keep it in cash**.
Go on the company course for the **new claims system**, however much I'd hate it.
feel: Like the **floor is tilting**, though the savings stop it turning into panic.
**Awake at night** running the numbers with Amira.
S1.quote: Checking claims is exactly what this card says goes first, and my whole team checks claims.
fieldNote: He reads the card as a direct hit, because his **team's core task** is checking.
His **resistance** gives way only to fear: he'd learn the system to keep his seat.
He worries most for **Bilal**, an older handler, which shows his loyalty to the team.

steps.text: Sign up fully with the union and go to its branch meetings
Move the joint savings into plain cash with Amira
Attend the company course on the new claims system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed by law, and I'd mean it. I'd sign every petition going and I'd tell people at work that the government should make firms keep staff on while it gets sorted. I'm not a marcher, but I'd march for this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by 2028, maybe sooner. Everything I do is thinking work, approvals and reports and deciding who gets which claim, and the card says all of that goes in 2 years. The robots coming 3 years later don't help me at all, because I don't do anything with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food and put every spare penny into the savings. I'd join whatever group of workers is pushing for a law to slow it down. And I'd ask Amira's ward manager what it actually takes to train as a healthcare assistant, because hands-on care gets those extra 3 years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the ground has gone and I'm the last one to notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira the night you realised your job was going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she might have to carry us for a while, and I'd hate saying it. My partner Amira has always said nurses would be the last ones standing, and I used to laugh. I wouldn't be laughing that night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new tech. Would 2 years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not into a fan of it, no. But 2 years is too short to be stubborn, so I'd learn whatever I had to. I just don't think learning it would save a manager's job when the thing can manage by itself.

say: I'd say AGI must be **slowed by law**, and firms should keep staff on meanwhile.
I'd **sign every petition** and, for once, I'd march too.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, because approvals, reports and allocation are all thinking work.
The extra **3 years for robots** don't help me, since I do nothing with my hands.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and save every spare penny.
Join the workers' groups pushing for a **law to slow it**.
Ask about training as a **healthcare assistant**, where hands-on work buys time.
feel: **Sick**, like the ground has gone and I'm the last to notice.
S2.quote: My partner Amira has always said nurses would be the last ones standing, and I used to laugh.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** outright, even with nine months saved.
He sees his work as **all thinking**, so the robot delay is no shield for him.
His partner's **nursing job** becomes the household's safety net, which pains him.

steps.text: Cut household spending down to rent, food and bills
Save every spare penny into the joint account
Join the campaign for a law slowing AI job cuts
Ask the ward manager about healthcare assistant training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them to write the rules before it lands. At work I'd push for a written promise on retraining for anyone whose role goes. I'd say the same at the union meeting and I'd say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 5 years is just enough to make me put it off, and that's my problem. I know myself. I'd tell myself 2031 is ages away and keep doing the Friday spreadsheet until it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd force myself to make a plan with dates on it. This year I'd save harder, the full nine months up to twelve. Next year I'd start an evening course in something hands-on, probably the healthcare route Amira keeps talking about, because the robots for that come around 2034, not 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then worse the closer it gets. Like a dentist appointment you booked a year ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the money for that course come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the savings, and I'd rather that than spend it on a holiday. We'd skip the trip to see my cousin this summer. Amira wouldn't love it, but she'd understand the reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies and the government, both of them, for letting it run without rules. My company makes a profit every year and still cut the north team. If they get a machine that does my job, they won't share a penny of what they save unless someone makes them.

say: I'd say we should use the time to **write the rules** before AGI lands.
I'd push for a **written promise** on retraining for anyone whose role goes.
think: Five years is long enough for me to **put it off**, and I know that about myself.
I'd keep filling in the **Friday spreadsheet** until it was too late.
do: Raise our savings from **nine months to twelve** this year.
Start an **evening course** in healthcare next year, paid from savings.
Skip the **summer trip** to see my cousin to cover the course.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, getting worse as 2031 comes closer.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself 2031 is ages away and keep doing the Friday spreadsheet until it's too late.
fieldNote: He openly admits his **resistance** would make him delay, so he sets himself dates.
He blames **companies and government** for letting change run without rules.
He still expects his role to go, so 5 years buys **planning time**, not safety.

steps.text: Build the savings up from nine to twelve months
Start an evening healthcare course next year
Skip the summer trip to visit his cousin
Push the union for a written retraining promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it properly, with training paid for by the firms that profit. I'd say that at work, and I'd vote for whoever promised it. It's the only one of these pictures where I'd sound hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 37 in 2036, so I'd still have a long career left to fill. My job goes in the end, the same as the others. But 10 years means I can switch while I'm young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep my job and keep saving. Around 2028 I'd start a part-time nursing degree, because Amira says the hospital pays some of the fees. By 2033 I'd want to be on a ward, with hands-on work that the robots don't reach until about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. It's a long road, but I can see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really leave management for a ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if I had the time to do it properly. My mum was a carer, and I've always felt a bit guilty that I went into an office. It's odd, but ten years would let me finally do the job my mum did as a carer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in waiting until 2028 to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else has the same idea and the courses fill up. I'd keep an eye on it. If the queue gets long, I'd start sooner.

say: I'd say ten years is time for **training paid by** the firms that profit.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised that, and sound hopeful for once.
think: My job still **goes in the end**, but I'd only be 37 by 2036.
A decade lets me **switch careers** while I'm young enough to start again.
do: Keep my job and **keep saving** for the first few years.
Start a **part-time nursing degree** around 2028, with fees partly paid by the hospital.
Aim to be on a **ward by 2033**, ahead of the robots.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frightened, because I can see the end of the road.
S4.quote: Ten years would let me finally do the job my mum did as a carer.
fieldNote: The long warning turns his **resistance** into a slow, deliberate career plan.
His mother's **caring work** gives the switch to nursing a personal meaning.
He'd still watch for **crowded courses**, a sign he isn't fully relaxed.

steps.text: Keep the claims job and keep saving until 2028
Start a part-time nursing degree around 2028
Vote for parties promising firm-paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd lose a job I'm good at with no time to become anything else. What would help is a law that makes big firms keep people on and pay for retraining for a couple of years, so the change doesn't land all at once on people like Bilal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how odd it feels that my partner's job is the safe one now. Amira works nights and gets paid less than me. In every one of these pictures, the person who lifts patients is safer than the person who signs off the claims.

headlineQuote: In every one of these pictures, the person who lifts patients is safer than the person who signs off the claims.
portrait: Yusuf is a 27-year-old **claims team manager** at a large insurer, living with Amira, a nurse.
He has about **nine months saved** and never uses AI tools, preferring the work he knows.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau but anxious once checking tasks start moving to software.
He expects to **lose his job** by 2028 in the fastest picture and would lean on Amira.
With more warning he'd **retrain into nursing**, following his mother's caring work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his job would go with **no time** to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** making big firms keep staff on and **pay for retraining** for a couple of years.
